programs.name: On-Campus Medical Office Building Financing
programs.description: Medical office buildings located on or immediately adjacent to a hospital campus, anchored by health system tenants under long-term net leases. The most creditworthy segment of the medical office market. Health system credit (often investment grade) and mission-critical location drive the tightest cap rates and the most competitive lender pricing in the healthcare real estate sector.
programs.typical_deal_range: $15M to $200M+ for portfolio or campus transactions
typical_stack: Permanent loan: life insurance company (most competitive) for stabilized with health system anchor
CMBS: active for $10M and above with investment-grade or near-investment-grade health system credit
Bridge: debt fund or bank for transitional or lease-up situations ahead of permanent takeout
Sale-leaseback: health system monetization of owned campus assets

key_features.tenant_profile: Hospital-affiliated physician groups, health system employed physicians, imaging and diagnostic services, surgery centers co-located with hospital
key_features.typical_lease_term: 10 to 20 years NNN, often with health system guaranty
key_features.building_specs: Medical-grade HVAC, reinforced floors for imaging equipment, exam room layouts, ADA accessibility throughout, hospital-level electrical capacity
key_features.most_competitive_lender: Life insurance companies: lowest spreads in the capital markets for on-campus with health system credit
key_features.ltv_ranges: 60 to 70 percent life co, 65 to 75 percent CMBS, pricing tightens significantly with investment-grade health system anchor
key_features.rate_environment_2026: Life co 125 to 175 over 10-year for investment-grade anchor, CMBS 175 to 250 over, bank 150 to 250 over

seo.meta_template: On-campus medical office building financing in {city}. Life company, CMBS, and health system sale-leaseback capital for hospital-affiliated MOB acquisitions and refinances.

programs.name: Off-Campus Medical Office Financing
programs.description: Medical office buildings in suburban locations away from hospital campuses, typically serving specialty physician groups, multi-specialty clinics, urgent care, dental, physical therapy, and outpatient diagnostic services. More diverse tenant mix than on-campus, with higher rollover risk and greater underwriting scrutiny on lease term remaining and tenant credit.
typical_stack: Permanent loan: community bank or regional bank for stabilized suburban MOB with diverse tenant roster
CMBS: active for $10M and above with strong occupancy and credit tenant anchors
Life insurance company: selective for larger off-campus assets with credit-tenant anchor
SBA 504 for owner-occupant physician group or small clinic acquisition
Bridge: debt fund for value-add or lease-up suburban medical office

key_features.tenant_profile: Specialty physician groups (orthopedics, cardiology, oncology), multi-specialty clinics, urgent care, dental groups, physical therapy, lab and diagnostic services
key_features.typical_lease_term: 5 to 10 years NNN or modified gross, shorter than on-campus with personal guaranty from physician owners
key_features.building_specs: Medical-grade HVAC, higher-than-standard electrical capacity, plumbing for clinical sinks, ADA-compliant, sometimes with imaging equipment rooms
key_features.most_competitive_lender: Community and regional banks for stabilized off-campus with diverse physician tenancy, SBA for owner-occupant
key_features.ltv_ranges: 65 to 75 percent community bank, 70 to 75 percent CMBS for stabilized, up to 90 percent SBA 504 owner-occupant
key_features.rate_environment_2026: Community bank 200 to 325 over 10-year or floating, CMBS 225 to 325 over, SBA fixed for owner-occupant

seo.meta_template: Off-campus medical office financing in {city}. Bank, CMBS, and SBA lenders for suburban medical office acquisitions, refinances, and owner-occupant physician practices.

programs.name: Outpatient Surgery Center Financing
programs.description: Ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) and outpatient surgery facilities performing same-day surgical procedures outside of hospital settings. Medicare and state licensing are critical underwriting variables. High revenue-per-square-foot and strong cash flow from insurance reimbursements underpin asset values. Lenders who understand ASC licensing, reimbursement structures, and physician ownership requirements are a narrow set.
programs.typical_deal_range: $5M to $40M total capitalization for real estate component
typical_stack: SBA 7(a) or 504 for physician-owned ASC acquisition with owner-occupant structure
Bridge: specialty healthcare debt fund for acquisition and stabilization
Permanent loan: community bank or regional bank with healthcare lending desk
Life company or CMBS: selective for large multi-specialty ASC with institutional operator (USPI, Surgery Partners, Envision)

key_features.tenant_profile: Physician-owned ASC partnerships, institutional ASC operators, hospital health system joint ventures
key_features.building_specs: OR suites with medical gas, dedicated HVAC, specialized electrical, sterile processing, recovery rooms, procedure rooms, Class B or Class C shell space can be converted
key_features.licensing_complexity: State ASC license required, Medicare certification required for reimbursement, AAAHC or JCAHO accreditation typical
key_features.most_competitive_lender: SBA 7(a) or 504 for physician owner-users, specialty healthcare debt funds for institutional operators
key_features.ltv_ranges: Up to 90 percent SBA for owner-occupant, 65 to 75 percent community bank, 65 to 70 percent specialty healthcare debt fund
key_features.rate_environment_2026: SBA fixed for owner-operator, community bank SOFR plus 250 to 375, specialty healthcare fund SOFR plus 400 to 600

seo.meta_template: Outpatient surgery center financing in {city}. SBA, specialty healthcare lenders, and bank capital for ambulatory surgery center acquisitions, construction, and physician owner-users.

cities.name: Los Angeles
cities.market_notes: Los Angeles is one of the deepest medical office markets in the country, anchored by Cedars-Sinai, UCLA Health, USC Keck, Kaiser Permanente, and Providence. On-campus MOBs adjacent to Cedars-Sinai in Beverly Grove and UCLA Medical Center in Westwood command the tightest cap rates in the Western US. Suburban medical office is dense in the San Fernando Valley, South Bay, and San Gabriel Valley, serving a population of 10 million.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies are highly competitive for on-campus MOBs anchored by Cedars-Sinai and UCLA-affiliated tenants. CMBS active for mid-market stabilized assets across LA County. California-based regional banks are the dominant off-campus and outpatient surgery center lenders. SBA 504 is the primary financing vehicle for physician-owned practices and ASC owner-users.
cities.submarkets: Beverly Grove and West Hollywood near Cedars-Sinai, Westwood and Brentwood near UCLA, Torrance and South Bay, Pasadena and San Gabriel Valley, Sherman Oaks and Encino, Burbank and Glendale

cities.name: Dallas
cities.market_notes: Dallas is one of the most active medical office markets in the country, with major health systems including UT Southwestern, Baylor Scott and White, Parkland Health, Texas Health Resources, and HCA Healthcare driving on-campus and affiliated off-campus demand. The Medical District near downtown Dallas and the growing suburban corridors of Frisco, Plano, and Southlake are among the most active medical office development submarkets in Texas.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life companies highly competitive for on-campus and affiliated MOBs with UT Southwestern and Baylor Scott and White credit. CMBS active for mid-market stabilized MOBs across the DFW metro. Regional Texas banks and community lenders dominant for off-campus physician practice buildings and ASC owner-users. SBA 504 active for physician groups acquiring their own space.
cities.submarkets: Dallas Medical District and Uptown, Frisco and The Colony, Plano and Allen, Southlake and Colleyville, North Dallas and Addison, Fort Worth Medical District

cities.name: Houston
cities.market_notes: Houston's Texas Medical Center is the world's largest medical complex, anchoring an enormous on-campus and adjacent medical office market. Beyond the TMC, suburban medical office is active in Sugar Land, The Woodlands, Katy, and Pearland as health systems extend outpatient networks to serve Houston's sprawling suburban population. ASC development has been particularly active in high-income suburban markets like Tanglewood and West University Place.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies aggressively compete for on-campus MOBs adjacent to Texas Medical Center and major health system affiliates. CMBS active for suburban stabilized assets. Regional Texas banks and national bank healthcare desks active on construction and suburban MOB lending. SBA 504 used for physician owner-operators and ASC acquisitions across the market.
cities.submarkets: Texas Medical Center and Museum District, Sugar Land and Missouri City, The Woodlands and Conroe, Katy and Cinco Ranch, Pearland and Friendswood, Tanglewood and West University Place

cities.name: Chicago
cities.market_notes: Chicago has one of the largest and most sophisticated medical office markets in the country, anchored by Northwestern Medicine, Rush University Medical Center, University of Chicago Medicine, Advocate Aurora Health, and NorthShore University Health. On-campus MOBs along the Magnificent Mile medical corridor and in the Oak Park-Evanston suburban ring are highly sought by institutional investors. Suburban medical office is active in the North Shore, western suburbs, and south suburban Cook County.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies are the most competitive for on-campus Northwestern and Rush-affiliated MOBs. CMBS conduits active for suburban stabilized assets in the $10M to $50M range. Midwest regional banks and Chicago-based community lenders dominant for off-campus physician practice buildings. Specialty healthcare debt funds active for ASC acquisitions and operator-driven deals.
cities.submarkets: Streeterville and Gold Coast near Northwestern, Oak Park and River Forest, Evanston and Wilmette North Shore, Naperville and Downers Grove, Schaumburg and Hoffman Estates, Orland Park and Tinley Park

cities.name: Atlanta
cities.market_notes: Atlanta is a major Southeast healthcare hub anchored by Emory Healthcare, Piedmont Healthcare, Wellstar Health System, Northside Hospital, and Children's Healthcare of Atlanta. On-campus and affiliated MOBs in Midtown (Emory-adjacent) and North Atlanta (Northside and Piedmont corridors) command institutional pricing. Suburban medical office development is active in Cherokee, Forsyth, and Paulding counties as health systems extend outpatient networks into the growing northern suburbs.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life companies actively quote on-campus and Emory-affiliated MOBs in Midtown and Buckhead. CMBS conduits active for mid-market suburban stabilized medical office. Southeast regional banks and Atlanta-based community lenders the primary off-campus and physician-practice lenders. Specialty healthcare debt funds provide ASC acquisition and bridge capital across the metro.
cities.submarkets: Midtown Atlanta and Emory Point, Buckhead and Sandy Springs, Alpharetta and Roswell, Marietta and Kennesaw, Johns Creek and Duluth, Peachtree City and Henry County

cities.name: Phoenix
cities.market_notes: Phoenix is one of the fastest-growing medical office markets in the country, supported by the Mayo Clinic Arizona campus in Scottsdale, Banner Health, Dignity Health, Valleywise Health, and HonorHealth. On-campus MOBs adjacent to the Mayo Clinic and Banner University Medical Center are the premier assets in the market. The East Valley (Gilbert, Chandler, Mesa) is seeing strong suburban medical office development tied to population growth.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life companies selectively compete for on-campus assets adjacent to Mayo Clinic and Banner campuses. CMBS active for mid-market stabilized suburban MOBs. Arizona-based regional banks and Western regional lenders active on construction and off-campus acquisitions. SBA 504 widely used by Arizona physician groups acquiring suburban practice buildings.
cities.submarkets: Scottsdale Healthcare Corridor near Mayo Clinic, Gilbert and Queen Creek, Chandler and Ahwatukee, Mesa and Tempe, North Phoenix and Anthem, Surprise and Buckeye

cities.name: New York
cities.market_notes: New York City's medical office building market is supported by one of the largest and most dense patient populations in the country, with major health systems including NYU Langone, NewYork-Presbyterian, Mount Sinai, and Northwell Health continuously expanding their ambulatory care footprints across all five boroughs and into suburban submarkets like Westchester and Long Island. Off-campus MOB demand is particularly strong as health systems push outpatient volume to lower-cost settings, with Class A medical office space in Manhattan and Brooklyn commanding premium rents and maintaining occupancy above 90% in well-located buildings. Lenders are generally constructive on stabilized, health-system-anchored assets but remain cautious on speculative development given elevated construction costs, high land values, and the complexity of navigating New York's regulatory environment.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and regional banks including Signature successor institutions, Valley National, and New York Private Bank are among the most active lenders for medical office deals in the New York metro, attracted by strong credit tenancy and recession-resistant cash flows. Life companies are selectively providing long-term fixed-rate financing on larger, institutional-quality on-campus and health-system-anchored MOBs in Manhattan and the surrounding suburbs.
cities.submarkets: Midtown Manhattan, Upper East Side, Brooklyn Heights, Flushing (Queens), The Bronx (Mott Haven/Fordham), White Plains (Westchester), Garden City (Long Island), Jersey City

cities.name: Miami
cities.market_notes: Miami's medical office building market benefits from strong population growth fueled by Northeast migration and a large, expanding Latino population with robust healthcare utilization rates, driving consistent demand for outpatient and specialty care facilities. Occupancy across established medical corridors in Coral Gables, Doral, and the Brickell health district remains tight, with vacancy rates for institutional-quality MOBs generally below 8 percent. Development activity is picking up with several off-campus outpatient facilities in planning or construction phases, though rising construction costs and high land prices are constraining new supply and keeping lender interest focused on stabilized assets.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks such as City National Bank of Florida and BankUnited are among the most active lenders for stabilized medical office deals in Miami, attracted by the strong tenant credit profiles and low vacancy in key submarkets. Debt funds have also been competitive on value-add and transitional MOB assets where conventional lenders pull back, particularly for deals in the 5 to 20 million dollar range tied to growing outpatient surgery center and specialty clinic operators.
cities.submarkets: Coral Gables, Doral, Brickell, Aventura, Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach, Miami Beach, Kendall

cities.name: Denver
cities.market_notes: Denver's medical office building market is supported by robust population growth across the metro, an aging demographic base, and the continued expansion of major health systems including UCHealth, SCL Health, and HCA HealthOne driving consistent demand for outpatient facilities. Occupancy rates for well-located medical office buildings have remained strong in the low-to-mid 90% range, particularly for on-campus and affiliated off-campus assets, while the development pipeline has moderated following a wave of construction completions that added outpatient inventory along key suburban corridors. Lenders are generally constructive on Denver medical office, though they are applying more scrutiny to speculative development deals and single-tenant assets with near-term lease expirations given broader office market softness creating some risk-off sentiment.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Vectra Bank, BOK Financial, and Colorado-based community lenders remain the most consistent capital source for Denver medical office acquisitions and refinances in the $5M to $30M range, offering competitive terms for creditworthy tenants and experienced healthcare operators. Life insurance companies and debt funds are selectively active on larger, multi-tenant assets anchored by health system credit tenants, particularly stabilized on-campus facilities where long-term lease structures support the underwriting.
cities.submarkets: Cherry Creek, Aurora, Lone Tree, Centennial, Lakewood, Highlands Ranch, Westminster, Broomfield

cities.name: Seattle
cities.market_notes: Seattle's medical office building market benefits from a rapidly growing and well-insured population base, with major health systems including UW Medicine, Swedish Health Services, and Providence expanding their ambulatory care footprints across the metro. Occupancy rates for Class A medical office buildings remain strong in the 90 to 95 percent range, particularly for off-campus facilities near dense residential corridors, as health systems push outpatient volume away from higher-cost hospital settings. The development pipeline is active but disciplined, concentrated around transit-accessible nodes and affluent suburbs, which keeps lender interest elevated for well-leased assets anchored by investment-grade health system tenants.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies and regional banks such as Banner Bank and Columbia Banking Group are the most competitive lenders for stabilized, credit-tenanted medical office buildings in Seattle, offering the tightest spreads for assets with long-term health system leases. Debt funds are stepping in for value-add acquisitions and construction bridge scenarios, particularly for off-campus outpatient surgery center developments where conventional lenders require higher stabilization before funding.
cities.submarkets: South Lake Union, Capitol Hill, Bellevue, Redmond, Tacoma, Shoreline, Renton, Kirkland

cities.name: San Diego
cities.market_notes: San Diego's medical office building market benefits from a large active-duty military and veteran population, a rapidly expanding life sciences corridor, and strong population growth in North County and South Bay submarkets that continues to drive outpatient care demand. Occupancy rates for medical office buildings in the metro have remained above 92% in core healthcare corridors, supported by UC San Diego Health, Scripps Health, Sharp HealthCare, and Kaiser Permanente anchoring tenant demand across multiple campuses. Geographic constraints limiting new supply, combined with high barriers to entry for development, have kept lenders constructive on well-leased medical office assets despite broader office sector headwinds.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Pacific Premier Bank and Banner Bank remain highly active for San Diego medical office building financing, particularly for credit-tenanted or health system-affiliated assets, while debt funds have stepped in aggressively for bridge and value-add opportunities in submarkets like Kearny Mesa and Rancho Bernardo where lease-up risk is manageable. Life companies are selectively placing long-term fixed-rate debt on stabilized, on-campus or adjacent MOBs with strong health system guarantees, drawn by the metro's income stability and limited new supply pipeline.
cities.submarkets: La Jolla, Kearny Mesa, Rancho Bernardo, Mission Valley, Chula Vista, Carlsbad, North County Inland, Downtown San Diego

cities.name: San Francisco
cities.market_notes: San Francisco's medical office building market benefits from a highly educated, affluent patient base and the presence of major health systems including UCSF Health, Sutter Health, and Kaiser Permanente, which anchor demand for both on-campus and off-campus MOB space. Mission Bay has emerged as a focal point for healthcare real estate activity given UCSF's expanding campus presence, while suburban nodes in San Mateo and Palo Alto continue to draw outpatient facility investment as providers follow population shifts away from the urban core. Lenders remain selectively cautious given elevated San Francisco construction costs, seismic compliance requirements, and broader urban office market headwinds, but strong credit tenancy from institutional health systems and historically low MOB vacancy rates continue to attract capital to well-located assets.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Life insurance companies and regional banks such as Bank of the West and Pacific Premier Bank are among the most active lenders for stabilized, credit-tenanted medical office buildings in the San Francisco metro, drawn by the strength of UCSF and Sutter Health-anchored deals. Debt funds are stepping in for value-add acquisitions and transitional assets where conventional lenders have pulled back, particularly for off-campus MOBs in suburban submarkets like San Mateo and Palo Alto where cash flow metrics are more compelling.
cities.submarkets: Mission Bay, SoMa, Palo Alto, San Mateo, Oakland, Walnut Creek, Marin County, Daly City

cities.name: Austin
cities.market_notes: Austin's rapid population growth, driven by major tech relocations and a surge in high-income residents, has created strong demand for outpatient medical services and specialist care, pushing medical office occupancy rates above 92% in many core submarkets. Health systems including Ascension Seton, St. David's HealthCare, and Baylor Scott and White have been aggressively expanding their outpatient footprints, supporting both on-campus and off-campus MOB development across the metro. The development pipeline remains active but is increasingly concentrated in suburban growth corridors like Cedar Park, Round Rock, and Georgetown, where population density is catching up with healthcare infrastructure needs.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks such as Frost Bank, Comerica, and Texas Capital Bank are among the most active lenders for medical office financing in Austin, drawn by strong occupancy fundamentals and creditworthy health system tenants. Debt funds and life companies are increasingly competing for larger single-tenant net lease MOBs anchored by investment-grade healthcare systems, offering aggressive terms on assets with long-term leases in place.
cities.submarkets: Round Rock, Cedar Park, Georgetown, The Domain, South Congress Corridor, North Austin, Pflugerville, Downtown Austin

cities.name: Nashville
cities.market_notes: Nashville stands as one of the most active medical office building markets in the Southeast, anchored by a dense concentration of major health systems including HCA Healthcare, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and Ascension Saint Thomas, all of which drive consistent demand for both on-campus and off-campus MOB space. Occupancy rates across the metro have remained above 92% in core submarkets, with particular strength in Brentwood and Franklin where physician group consolidation and suburban population growth are fueling absorption of new product. The development pipeline remains elevated but disciplined, with most new deliveries pre-leased to health system-affiliated tenants, a factor that continues to attract institutional lender interest despite broader commercial real estate headwinds.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Pinnacle Financial Partners and Avenue Bank affiliates remain highly active for stabilized MOB loans in Nashville given their familiarity with local health system credit and strong deposit relationships with physician groups. Life companies such as Nationwide and Principal have also shown increased appetite for Class A, long-term net-leased MOBs in Brentwood and Franklin, drawn by the market's investment-grade tenant profiles and low vacancy fundamentals.
cities.submarkets: Brentwood, Franklin, Murfreesboro, Green Hills, Midtown Nashville, Cool Springs, Berry Hill, Germantown

cities.name: Tampa
cities.market_notes: Tampa's medical office building market benefits from one of the fastest-growing population bases in the Southeast, with consistent in-migration from the Northeast and Midwest driving strong demand for outpatient healthcare services across the metro. Occupancy rates for well-located MOBs in Tampa remain above 92%, with tenants such as BayCare Health System, AdventHealth, and HCA Florida anchoring both on-campus and off-campus assets and providing lenders with confidence in rent stability. Development activity is concentrated in suburban growth corridors like Brandon, Wesley Chapel, and the Westshore medical district, though construction costs and insurance premiums have moderated new starts and kept competitive supply in check.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Regions Bank, Truist, and Florida-based community lenders are the most active financing sources for Tampa MOBs, drawn by strong credit tenants and the metro's population growth fundamentals, while debt funds are stepping in aggressively for value-add acquisitions and construction bridge situations where traditional banks have pulled back on leverage. Life companies are selectively pursuing stabilized, credit-tenanted on-campus MOBs at conservative loan-to-value ratios, particularly for assets affiliated with BayCare or AdventHealth systems.
cities.submarkets: Westshore, Brandon, Wesley Chapel, New Tampa, St. Petersburg, Clearwater, Downtown Tampa, South Tampa

cities.name: Charlotte
cities.market_notes: Charlotte's medical office building market is supported by rapid population growth exceeding 2% annually, a young and expanding workforce, and the ongoing buildout of Atrium Health and Novant Health ambulatory networks across the metro. Off-campus MOB occupancy remains above 93% in key suburban corridors as both health systems aggressively push outpatient care to lower-cost settings, with notable development activity in Ballantyne, University City, and the broader I-485 loop. Lenders are broadly constructive on Charlotte MOB given the metro's strong demographic tailwinds, though construction cost pressures and a meaningful new supply pipeline in certain submarkets are prompting more conservative underwriting on speculative development deals.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks headquartered or with strong Charlotte presences, including Bank of America and Truist Financial, are among the most active lenders on stabilized and pre-leased medical office deals given their deep local market knowledge and appetite for healthcare-credit tenants. Debt funds and life companies are also competitive on larger, credit-anchored MOBs and outpatient surgery centers, particularly assets with long-term Atrium Health or Novant Health leases that justify lower cap rate assumptions.
cities.submarkets: Ballantyne, University City, South Charlotte, Concord, Huntersville, Pineville, Uptown, Midtown

cities.name: Minneapolis
cities.market_notes: Minneapolis-St. Paul is one of the strongest medical office building markets in the Midwest, anchored by a dense concentration of major health systems including Mayo Clinic, Allina Health, M Health Fairview, and HealthPartners, which collectively drive consistent demand for both on-campus and off-campus outpatient facilities. Occupancy rates for medical office buildings across the metro have remained above 90% in core submarkets, supported by a highly educated and insured population base and strong per-capita healthcare spending. The development pipeline has been active particularly along suburban corridors in Eden Prairie, Bloomington, and Maple Grove, though rising construction costs have moderated speculative starts and kept lender appetite focused on credit-tenanted or health-system-affiliated assets.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including U.S. Bank, Associated Bank, and Bremer Bank are among the most active lenders for medical office building financing in Minneapolis, benefiting from deep local market knowledge and strong existing relationships with Twin Cities health systems. Life companies such as Principal Financial and Securian Financial, both headquartered in the metro, are also competitive on long-term fixed-rate financing for stabilized, credit-tenanted medical office assets, offering favorable terms that reflect their comfort with the market's strong healthcare sector fundamentals.
cities.submarkets: Bloomington, Eden Prairie, St. Paul, Downtown Minneapolis, Plymouth, Maple Grove, Minnetonka, Edina

cities.name: Portland
cities.market_notes: Portland's medical office building market benefits from a large and growing healthcare system anchored by OHSU, Providence Health, and Legacy Health, which continue to expand outpatient care networks across the metro to serve a population that has grown significantly over the past decade. Off-campus MOB demand remains strong as health systems push care closer to patients in suburban corridors like Beaverton and Hillsboro, keeping overall medical office occupancy in the low-to-mid 90s percent range for well-located assets. Lenders remain constructive on stabilized, health-system-affiliated assets but are exercising caution on speculative development and standalone single-tenant facilities given broader Pacific Northwest office market softness and lingering concerns about Portland's urban core economic recovery.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks including Banner Bank and Umpqua Bank remain among the most active lenders for Portland medical office deals, particularly for community health and outpatient surgery center financing where local market knowledge supports underwriting, while debt funds have stepped in to fill gaps on value-add and lease-up deals that life companies and CMBS lenders are currently bypassing due to elevated credit standards. Life companies remain selectively active for larger, long-term net-leased assets with strong health system credit tenancy in suburban submarkets.
cities.submarkets: Beaverton, Hillsboro, Lake Oswego, Lloyd District, Tualatin, Vancouver WA, Southwest Portland, Oregon City

cities.name: Las Vegas
cities.market_notes: Las Vegas is experiencing strong demand for medical office space driven by rapid population growth, significant in-migration from California, and a historically underserved healthcare infrastructure relative to its metro size. Occupancy rates for well-located MOBs remain tight, particularly in master-planned communities like Summerlin and Henderson, where suburban growth is generating new patient volumes for primary care, orthopedics, and outpatient surgery. Lenders are cautiously optimistic, attracted by demographic tailwinds and limited legacy supply, though some scrutinize the market's historical economic volatility tied to tourism and gaming cycles.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Debt funds and regional banks are the most active lenders for medical office building financing in Las Vegas right now, with debt funds offering flexible structures for value-add and newly constructed MOBs and regional banks like Western Alliance and Nevada State Bank providing competitive terms for established healthcare operators with strong occupancy. Life companies are selectively active on larger, credit-tenanted on-campus or health-system-anchored assets in Summerlin and Henderson where long-term lease structures meet their underwriting criteria.
cities.submarkets: Henderson, Summerlin, Spring Valley, Enterprise, North Las Vegas, Southwest Las Vegas, Green Valley

cities.name: Orlando
cities.market_notes: Orlando's medical office building market benefits from one of the fastest-growing populations in the Sun Belt, with the metro adding roughly 60,000 new residents annually and driving sustained demand for outpatient and specialty care facilities. Lake Nona's Medical City anchors a significant development pipeline, attracting health systems like UCF Health, Nemours, and AdventHealth, while off-campus MOB occupancy across the metro remains tight in the low-to-mid 90% range. Lenders are drawn to Orlando's favorable demographics and healthcare employment growth, though they are monitoring new supply concentrations around Lake Nona and underwriting rent growth conservatively given rising construction costs.
cities.active_lender_commentary: Regional banks and debt funds are the most active lenders for medical office building financing in Orlando right now, with institutions like Truist, Regions Bank, and TD Bank competing aggressively on stabilized on-campus and off-campus assets tied to credit health system tenants. Life companies are selectively active on larger, long-term net-leased MOBs above $10 million anchored by investment-grade healthcare operators, drawn by Florida's landlord-friendly legal environment and strong rent fundamentals.
cities.submarkets: Lake Nona, Winter Park, Altamonte Springs, Dr. Phillips, Kissimmee, Sand Lake Road Corridor, Downtown Orlando, Oviedo
